cover.title: Who Pays Who at the Salon?
cover.label: SALON

lines.text: Your stylist might be paying the salon.
lines.say: Your stylist might be paying the salon.

lines.text: Not the other way around. Nearly half of US hairstylists were self-employed in 2024, and the salon is often their landlord.
lines.say: Not the other way around. Nearly half of US hairstylists were self-employed in twenty twenty-four, and the salon is often their landlord.

lines.text: Salons usually use one of two models: commission or booth rent.
lines.say: Salons usually use one of two models: commission or booth rent.

lines.text: Say a stylist brings in $1,000 a week. At a 50% commission, they keep $500.
lines.say: Say a stylist brings in a thousand dollars a week. At a fifty percent commission, they keep five hundred.

lines.text: With a $300 booth rent, they keep $700, before supplies and taxes.
lines.say: With a three hundred dollar booth rent, they keep seven hundred, before supplies and taxes.

lines.text: Below $600 a week, commission pays more, even before a renter's other costs.
lines.say: Below six hundred a week, commission pays more, even before a renter's other costs.

lines.text: Renters also cover products, insurance, and the full 15.3% self-employment tax, with no paid time off.
lines.say: Renters also cover products, insurance, and the full fifteen point three percent self-employment tax, with no paid time off.

lines.text: In 2023, Census counted about 838,000 beauty businesses with no employees, versus 84,000 with staff.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-three, Census counted about eight hundred thirty-eight thousand beauty businesses with no employees, versus eighty-four thousand with staff.

lines.text: For stylists on payroll, median pay rose from $12.54 an hour in 2019 to $17.21 in 2025.
lines.say: For stylists on payroll, median pay rose from twelve fifty-four an hour in twenty nineteen to seventeen twenty-one in twenty twenty-five.

post.title: Your stylist might be paying the salon: booth rent vs commission
post.ig:
Your stylist might be paying the salon, not the other way around.
Nearly half of US hairstylists were self-employed in 2024 (BLS).
Salons usually earn either a commission (often 40% to 60% of what a stylist brings in) or booth rent.
Example: a $1,000 week at 50% commission leaves the stylist $500; with $300 booth rent, $700 before supplies and taxes. Break-even: $600 a week.
Census counted about 838,000 beauty businesses with no employees in 2023 vs about 84,000 salons with employees.
Sources: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and OEWS; Census (2023).
News and education, not financial advice.
